question: The most important bedside clinical feature distinguishing central from peripheral hypotonia in a floppy infant is the status of deep tendon reflexes.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is true. The reflex status is the key bedside differentiator: absent DTRs in a hypotonic infant = peripheral lower motor neurone lesion (consider SMA, neuropathy, NMJ disorder, myopathy); preserved DTRs with hypotonia = central origin (consider HIE, chromosomal disorders, metabolic conditions). The clinical pearl: an alert floppy infant with absent DTRs has a peripheral lesion until proven otherwise.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. In central hypotonia (lesion above the anterior horn cell — brain, spinal cord), deep tendon reflexes are PRESERVED or may be brisk, and are associated with cortical signs (poor alertness, seizures, feeding difficulties, abnormal tone distribution). In peripheral hypotonia (anterior horn cell, peripheral nerve, NMJ, muscle), deep tendon reflexes are ABSENT or markedly reduced, and the infant may be paradoxically alert. This reflex distinction is the most reliable bedside differentiator.
